summary: Defines the data collected for security auditing in healthcare applications, and the minimum attributes to capture, as an XML schema. It serves as a reference for developers of healthcare standards and applications and consolidates several existing sources.

plainLanguage.summary: Hospitals need a diary of who looked at patient records. This document sets out what to write down and in what format.

questions: xml schema for audit logs in healthcare
what is the rfc 3881 audit message structure
subtitle: Standard XML format for recording who accessed patient data and when.

tldr.problem: Healthcare systems need to track who accessed patient records, when, what action they took, and from where, to enforce privacy policies and investigate breaches. Different healthcare vendors use incompatible audit formats.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC defines a common XML schema for audit messages, with five categories: what happened (event ID, action, outcome), who did it (user ID, role), from where (network address), on which system (audit source ID), and what was accessed (patient ID, record type).
tldr.outcome: The schema consolidates viewpoints from HL7, DICOM, IHE, and ASTM E31, giving healthcare standards developers and application designers a common reference for security audit data.

facts.label: Data categories
facts.value: 5: event, participant, network, audit source, participant object

facts.label: Outcome values
facts.value: 4: success (0), minor failure (4), serious failure (8), major failure (12)

today: RFC 3881 is Informational. It serves as a reference standard that healthcare organizations can adopt or extend for their audit systems. While the RFC itself does not specify conformance requirements or binding standards, it consolidates requirements from multiple healthcare standards bodies (HL7, DICOM, IHE, ASTM) and provides a common schema that implementations can use to ensure interoperability and data portability across healthcare systems.

sections.title: Purpose and Scope
sections.content:
Healthcare organizations must be able to audit access to patient data to verify compliance with privacy and security policies and to establish accountability if data is accessed improperly. This RFC defines the format and minimum content of audit messages that healthcare application systems must generate and transmit to a central audit repository.

The document consolidates previously separate standards from Health Level 7 (HL7), DICOM imaging systems, Integrating the Healthcare Enterprise (IHE), and ASTM, providing a single reference point. It anticipates that the data will be collected from multiple heterogeneous systems and aggregated for querying and reporting.
sections.plainLanguage: Different healthcare systems all over the hospital need to report who accessed what data, when, and why. This document says what information they must all collect.

sections.title: Audit Data Model
sections.content:
Every audit message contains five categories of information:

  • Event Identification: what happened. The event ID identifies the action (e.g., a function name or menu item), the action code (Create, Read, Update, Delete, Execute), a timestamp in UTC, and an outcome indicator (success, minor failure, serious failure, or major failure).
  • Active Participant Identification: who did it. The user ID is required and unique within the audit source. Optional fields include the user's human name, alternative ID (for cross-system tracking), roles, and whether the user was the requestor or recipient of the action.
  • Network Access Point Identification: from where. The type (machine name, IP address, or telephone number) and ID of the device or network location.
  • Audit Source Identification: on which system. The audit source ID, enterprise site ID, and source type (end-user display, web server, application server, database server, security server, or network component).
  • Participant Object Identification: what was accessed. Optional but important for privacy audits: the type of object (person, system object, organization), its ID (medical record number, patient number, etc.), the life-cycle stage (origination, import, amendment, disclosure, etc.), and optionally the sensitivity (VIP, HIV status, etc.).
sections.plainLanguage: Every audit entry records: what happened, who did it, where they were, which system it happened on, and which patient's data was involved.

sections.title: Trigger Events and Use Cases
sections.content:
Audit messages are triggered by specific events. Security administration events include creation, modification, deletion, or querying of data definitions, function definitions, roles, user accounts, and access permissions. Audit administration events include enabling or disabling audited events, accessing audit data, and modifying or deleting audit data.

User access events are the most relevant to privacy: successful and failed sign-on attempts, sign-off, function invocation requiring permissions, and patient care data access. The RFC lists specific healthcare triggers including patient record creation/update/delete, encounter (visit) management, orders, medications, care protocols, and staff assignments. Not all triggers must be audited; healthcare organizations select which to enable based on their policies.
sections.plainLanguage: An audit record is created when someone logs in, looks at a patient file, changes an order, or modifies their access permissions. Different organizations choose which events matter to them.

sections.title: Data Definitions and Coding
sections.content:
Each element is defined with its purpose, whether it is required or optional, its format, and the values it can take. For example:

  • Event ID: required, coded value identifying the function. Attributes include CodeSystem (OID), CodeSystemName (human name), DisplayName, and OriginalText (what the user entered before translation to a code).
  • Event Action Code: optional, enumerated as C (Create), R (Read), U (Update), D (Delete), E (Execute).
  • Event Outcome Indicator: required, enumerated (0 = success, 4 = minor failure, 8 = serious failure, 12 = major failure).
  • Participant Object Type Code: optional, enumerated as Person, System Object, Organization, Other.
  • Participant Object ID Type Code: required when a participant object is identified; enumerated types include Medical Record Number, Patient Number, Encounter Number, User Identifier, and Report Name.

Many fields anticipate implementation-defined or standard vocabulary extensions. The schema allows multiple roles per user and multiple participant objects per event.
sections.plainLanguage: Each piece of information has a defined format and allowed values. For instance, action code is one of five letters, and outcome is a number from 0 to 12 indicating success or failure.

sections.title: XML Schema and Implementation
sections.content:
The RFC provides a complete XML Schema definition (W3C-compliant) for the AuditMessage element. The schema structures the data as nested elements and attributes. The root AuditMessage contains EventIdentification, one or more ActiveParticipant elements, one or more AuditSourceIdentification elements, and zero or more ParticipantObjectIdentification elements.

The schema is designed as a reference; healthcare standards organizations and application developers are expected to extend it for domain-specific requirements via schema localization. Organizations must document their conformance practices; this RFC does not define conformance requirements itself.

For efficient collection and transmission, the RFC recommends auditing at the transaction or record level, not at the individual attribute level. It also suggests filtering, aggregation, and summarization on each application system before transmission to a central repository, and selective auditing based on policy.
sections.plainLanguage: The data is formatted as XML that systems can parse and understand. Applications can add their own extensions for special cases, as long as the core information is there.
